Welcome

BPT Speaking Practice Test

This is an interactive practice page for the BPT L2 B1 Speaking Test.

Topics for this semester: Globalization, Human Rights, and Armed Conflict.

How the exam works

The exam is taken in groups of three students (A, B, C) and lasts approximately 13 minutes. It has 3 parts.

1
Part 1: Interview 4.5 min total / 1.5 min each
The interlocutor asks personal questions and questions about the course topics. You give your opinion and support it with at least 2 arguments.
2
Part 2: Question & Photo 4.5 min total / 1.5 min each
You get a question and two photographs. You must answer the question using the pictures as reference. You speak alone for about one minute.
3
Part 3: Group discussion 4 min for all three
The evaluator assigns each student ONE option to defend. You must defend your assigned position with strong arguments. This part is worth 5 points out of 20.

How to use this practice page

  • Click the tabs above to navigate between the three parts and the rubric.
  • Click Show model answer on any question only after you've tried to answer it on your own.
  • Use the floating Timer (bottom-right corner) to simulate exam pressure.
  • Review the Rubric tab and tick items in the self-check before the exam.
Part 1: 4.5 minutes

Interview questions

The interlocutor will ask you personal questions and questions about the three course topics. According to the rubric, you must clearly express your opinion AND support it with at least 2 arguments.

OAAC Structure: Opinion, 2 Arguments & Conclusion

The rubric requires you to give your opinion AND support it with at least 2 arguments. Use this 4-step structure for every answer.

1
1. Opinion
State your position clearly in one sentence. Use 'In my opinion...', 'I personally believe...', 'From my perspective...'
2
2. Argument 1 (with example)
Introduce your first reason with 'Firstly, ...' or 'First of all, ...' and support it with a real example using 'For example, ...'
3
3. Argument 2 (with example)
Add a second, different reason with 'Secondly, ...', 'Another reason is that ...' or 'On the other hand, ...' and give another example.
4
4. Conclusion
Close with a short summary. Use 'To sum up, ...', 'In conclusion, ...', 'So I would say that ...'

Key phrases for Part 1

Giving opinion

  • In my opinion, ...
  • From my perspective, ...
  • Personally, I believe that ...
  • From my point of view, ...
  • I'd say that ...
  • Honestly, I think ...

Connecting two arguments

  • Firstly, ... Secondly, ...
  • First of all, ... In addition, ...
  • On the one hand, ... On the other hand, ...
  • Another reason is that ...
  • Furthermore, ...
  • Moreover, ...

Giving reasons & examples

  • ... because ...
  • The main reason is that ...
  • For example, ...
  • For instance, ...
  • A clear example is ...
  • Take ... for example.

Concluding

  • To sum up, ...
  • In conclusion, ...
  • Overall, I think ...
  • All in all, ...
  • So, I would say that ...

Practice these as a warm-up. They usually come at the very beginning of the exam.

01Do you think globalization has more benefits than disadvantages?

Model answer (B1): Opinion, 2 Arguments Conclusion
In my opinion, globalization has more benefits than disadvantages overall. Firstly, it has allowed us to share knowledge, technology and culture across borders. For example, today we can study online with universities from anywhere in the world without leaving home. Secondly, it has created new economic opportunities, especially for young people who can now work remotely for international companies. A clear case is the growing tech industry in cities like Medellín. To sum up, although globalization has some negative effects on local businesses, the benefits are much greater.

02How has globalization changed the way people work in your country?

Model answer (B1): Opinion, 2 Arguments Conclusion
From my perspective, globalization has changed work in Colombia in two important ways. Firstly, many people now work remotely for foreign companies, which has created better-paid jobs, especially in technology and services. For instance, several of my friends work as freelancers for clients in the United States. Secondly, traditional local jobs have decreased because of international competition. A clear example is small farmers, who struggle to compete with imported products. In conclusion, globalization has brought new opportunities, but also new challenges for our workforce.

03Is migration a human right? Why or why not?

Model answer (B1): Opinion, 2 Arguments Conclusion
I personally believe migration should be considered a human right. Firstly, when people leave their countries because of war, persecution or extreme poverty, they are simply trying to survive. For example, many Venezuelans have come to Colombia looking for safety and work, and we cannot judge them for that. Secondly, migration also enriches the receiving country with new ideas, talents and cultural diversity. Take Canada, for instance, where immigrants have helped build a strong economy. To sum up, migration is a fundamental right that benefits both migrants and host societies.

04Do you think the world is becoming too dependent on global companies?

Model answer (B1): Opinion, 2 Arguments Conclusion
Yes, I do think the world is becoming dangerously dependent on a few global companies. Firstly, in technology, almost everyone uses the same platforms like Google, WhatsApp or Amazon, which gives these corporations enormous power over our personal data. For example, a single decision from Meta can affect millions of users worldwide. Secondly, this concentration also damages small local businesses, which cannot compete on prices or visibility. A clear case is small bookshops disappearing because of Amazon. In conclusion, we should support local alternatives to reduce this dependency.

05How does globalization affect local cultures and traditions?

Model answer (B1): Opinion, 2 Arguments & Conclusion
In my view, globalization has both positive and negative effects on local cultures. Firstly, on the positive side, people from different countries can share their music, food and traditions much more easily. For example, K-pop and Japanese anime are now popular in Colombia thanks to streaming platforms. Secondly, on the negative side, many young people prefer foreign culture and forget their own roots. A clear example is how some Colombian teenagers know more about American holidays than about local festivals. So, the challenge is staying open to other cultures without losing our identity.

06Should countries protect local businesses from international competition?

Model answer (B1): Opinion, 2 Arguments & Conclusion
Yes, I believe countries should protect their local businesses, but in a smart way. Firstly, small producers cannot compete against multinationals that have huge budgets and lower costs. For example, Colombian coffee farmers need government support to survive against big international brands. Secondly, protecting local businesses also helps preserve jobs and traditional knowledge in the country. A clear case is artisanal industries in small towns that depend on government incentives. In conclusion, protection is necessary, but it must be balanced with openness to international trade.

07How has technology contributed to globalization?

Model answer (B1): Opinion, 2 Arguments & Conclusion
In my opinion, technology has been the main engine of globalization. Firstly, the internet and smartphones have made instant communication possible between any two points on the planet. For example, I can have a video call with a friend in Australia in just a few seconds. Secondly, technology has also transformed international trade and business. A clear case is e-commerce platforms like Amazon or AliExpress, which let small companies sell anywhere in the world. To sum up, without technology, globalization as we know it today would simply be impossible.

08Do you think globalization is making the world more equal or more unequal?

Model answer (B1): Opinion, 2 Arguments & Conclusion
From my point of view, globalization has actually made the world more unequal. Firstly, although some countries have grown economically, the gap between rich and poor has increased within most societies. For example, multinational CEOs earn millions while their workers in developing countries earn very little. Secondly, big companies often locate in poor countries to pay low wages, which keeps inequality alive. A clear case is the textile industry in Asia. In conclusion, globalization could reduce inequality, but only if governments distribute its benefits more fairly.

09What role do social media play in connecting cultures worldwide?

Model answer (B1): Opinion, 2 Arguments & Conclusion
Social media play a very powerful role in connecting cultures today, in my opinion. Firstly, platforms like Instagram and TikTok let people share their traditions, languages and lifestyles with millions of users instantly. For instance, I have learned about Korean culture mainly through TikTok videos. Secondly, social media also help minorities and indigenous voices reach a global audience for the first time. A clear example is indigenous Colombian creators who now share their language online. In conclusion, social media are an excellent tool for cultural exchange when we use them responsibly.

10Is globalization mostly a positive or a negative force for developing countries?

Model answer (B1): Opinion, 2 Arguments & Conclusion
In my opinion, globalization is mostly positive for developing countries, although it has clear risks. Firstly, it has brought foreign investment, technology and new jobs to places that needed them. For example, several international companies have opened offices in Bogotá and Medellín, creating thousands of jobs. Secondly, it has also given local talent access to global markets, especially through the internet. A clear case is Colombian designers and artists who now sell their work worldwide. To sum up, developing countries benefit from globalization as long as they protect their workers and industries.

01Do you believe that human rights are universal, or do they depend on culture?

Model answer (B1): Opinion, 2 Arguments & Conclusion
I personally believe human rights are universal because they protect basic things every human being needs. Firstly, no culture should accept violations like torture, slavery or child marriage, even if they appear in tradition. For example, the right to life and freedom from violence is non-negotiable in any society. Secondly, although some rights may apply differently in each context, the core idea is the same everywhere. A clear case is the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, signed by almost every country in the world. In conclusion, human rights must be universal, even if their application adapts to local realities.

02What do you think is the most important human right?

Model answer (B1): Opinion, 2 Arguments & Conclusion
For me, the most important human right is the right to education. Firstly, education makes all the other rights possible because it teaches people what their rights are and how to defend them. For example, an educated person can understand laws, vote with criteria and demand justice. Secondly, education is the most powerful tool to break the cycle of poverty and inequality. A clear case is countries like Finland, where universal education has produced one of the most equal societies in the world. To sum up, education is the foundation that supports all other human rights.

03Do you think governments should prioritize human rights over national security?

Model answer (B1): Opinion, 2 Arguments & Conclusion
Yes, in my opinion governments should never sacrifice human rights for security. Firstly, when a country violates rights in the name of security, it loses the trust of its own citizens. For example, when governments arrest people without trial, it generates fear instead of safety. Secondly, real security cannot be built on injustice; it only creates more violence in the long term. A clear case is countries that have used 'anti-terrorism laws' to silence political opponents, which has led to more conflict. In conclusion, true security is built on respect for human rights, not on their violation.

04How can individuals contribute to the protection of human rights?

Model answer (B1): Opinion, 2 Arguments & Conclusion
I think individuals can contribute to protecting human rights in many small but powerful ways. Firstly, we can start in our daily life by respecting others and speaking up when we see discrimination. For example, defending a classmate who is being bullied is already a way to defend human rights. Secondly, we can take action at a wider level by supporting NGOs, signing petitions or even voting consciously. A clear case is the global response to the Black Lives Matter movement, which started with individual actions. In conclusion, change doesn't only come from governments, but from each of us.

05Do you think freedom of speech should have any limits?

Model answer (B1): Opinion, 2 Arguments & Conclusion
Yes, I do think freedom of speech should have some limits, although it is a fundamental right. Firstly, speech that promotes hate or violence against specific groups can cause real harm to people's lives. For example, Nazi propaganda or racist speech in social media has led to attacks on minorities. Secondly, fake news that puts public health or democracy at risk should also be regulated. A clear case is the misinformation about vaccines during the pandemic, which cost many lives. In conclusion, freedom of speech is essential, but it must come with responsibility.

06Are human rights adequately protected in Colombia?

Model answer (B1) · Opinion + 2 Arguments + Conclusion
Honestly, I think human rights are not fully protected in Colombia yet. Firstly, although we have a strong Constitution, in practice many social leaders and activists are still being killed every year. For example, Colombia is one of the most dangerous countries in the world for environmental defenders. Secondly, certain communities like indigenous and Afro-Colombian groups continue to face structural discrimination. A clear case is the lack of basic services in regions like the Pacific coast. In conclusion, our laws are good on paper, but a lot of work is needed to apply them in real life.

07How can education promote human rights?

Model answer (B1) · Opinion + 2 Arguments + Conclusion
In my opinion, education promotes human rights in two essential ways. Firstly, it teaches children from a young age what their rights are and how to respect the rights of others. For example, in schools we can discuss real cases of discrimination and learn how to react to them. Secondly, education builds critical thinking, which protects citizens from manipulation and propaganda. A clear case is countries with strong civic education, where democratic participation is much higher. To sum up, an educated society is much harder to oppress, so education is one of the best tools we have.

08Do you think social media help or harm human rights?

Model answer (B1) · Opinion + 2 Arguments + Conclusion
From my perspective, social media both help and harm human rights, depending on how we use them. Firstly, on the positive side, they allow activists to share information and organize movements quickly. A clear example was the global response to George Floyd's murder, which spread thanks to social media. Secondly, on the negative side, they can also spread hate speech, fake news and discrimination very fast. For instance, online harassment has affected the mental health of many young people. In conclusion, social media are a powerful tool, but they need clear rules and responsible use.

09What should be done to fight discrimination?

Model answer (B1) · Opinion + 2 Arguments + Conclusion
I believe fighting discrimination requires action from both governments and citizens. Firstly, governments must create strong anti-discrimination laws and actually enforce them. For example, countries like Canada have specific institutions that protect minorities and punish discrimination. Secondly, society must change attitudes through education, media and culture. A clear case is the inclusion of more diverse stories in films and schoolbooks, which helps younger generations grow up with respect. To sum up, fighting discrimination is a long-term process that needs commitment from the whole society.

10Do you think economic rights (housing, food) are as important as civil rights?

Model answer (B1) · Opinion + 2 Arguments + Conclusion
Yes, in my opinion economic rights are just as important as civil rights, because they protect human dignity. Firstly, you cannot truly enjoy freedom if you are hungry or homeless. For example, a person who can vote but cannot eat is not really free in any meaningful sense. Secondly, when basic needs are not covered, social problems like crime and inequality also increase. A clear case is countries where the lack of housing has produced deep social tensions. In conclusion, real human rights must include both political freedom and basic economic security.

01Do you think the Truth Commission in Colombia is necessary to achieve peace?

Model answer (B1) · Opinion + 2 Arguments + Conclusion
Yes, I strongly believe the Truth Commission is necessary to achieve real peace in Colombia. Firstly, peace cannot be built on silence; the country needs to know what happened, who was responsible and why. For example, listening to victims' stories helps society understand the human cost of the conflict. Secondly, the truth is the only way to prevent these atrocities from being repeated in the future. A clear case is South Africa, where the Truth Commission helped the country move forward after apartheid. In conclusion, the Truth Commission is a key step toward genuine reconciliation.

02How important is it to listen to victims in a post-conflict society?

Model answer (B1) · Opinion + 2 Arguments + Conclusion
In my opinion, listening to victims is one of the most important parts of building peace. Firstly, victims need to be heard and recognized publicly to begin their healing process. For example, public hearings in Colombia have allowed many families to share their stories for the first time. Secondly, their testimonies also help the rest of society understand the real impact of the war. A clear case is the JEP, where victims have spoken directly to former combatants. To sum up, without the voice of victims, there can be no true reconciliation.

03Can forgiveness really heal a country after armed conflict?

Model answer (B1) · Opinion + 2 Arguments + Conclusion
In my opinion, forgiveness is part of the healing process, but it is not enough on its own. Firstly, forgiveness has a powerful effect because it allows people to move forward without hatred. For example, some Colombian victims have publicly forgiven former combatants in deeply moving ceremonies. Secondly, however, forgiveness must come together with truth, justice and reparation. A clear case is countries where forgiveness was forced too early, and conflicts came back later. To sum up, forgiveness helps a lot, but real healing requires structural changes too.

04Do you think Colombia has truly entered a post-conflict era?

Model answer (B1) · Opinion + 2 Arguments + Conclusion
Honestly, I think Colombia is in a transition, but not fully in a post-conflict era yet. Firstly, the peace agreement with the FARC was a huge step forward and reduced violence significantly in many regions. For example, certain rural areas that were dangerous before are now safer for residents. Secondly, however, other armed groups remain active and new forms of violence have appeared. A clear case is the situation in places like Cauca, Catatumbo and Chocó. In conclusion, we have made important progress, but real and complete peace is still a process.

05What role should former combatants play in society?

Model answer (B1) · Opinion + 2 Arguments + Conclusion
I believe former combatants should have the chance to reintegrate into society as productive citizens. Firstly, they need real opportunities like education, employment and psychological support to rebuild their lives. For example, several reintegration programs in Colombia have helped ex-combatants start small businesses. Secondly, society also needs to learn to accept them again, otherwise reintegration fails. A clear case is communities where former fighters and victims have begun to work together in peace projects. In conclusion, society should give them a fair second chance, with accountability for past actions.

06How effective do you think peace agreements are in your country?

Model answer (B1) · Opinion + 2 Arguments + Conclusion
From my point of view, peace agreements have been partially effective in Colombia. Firstly, the agreement with the FARC has clearly reduced violence in many regions and brought political participation for former guerrillas. For example, several ex-combatants now hold seats in Congress. Secondly, however, many promises about rural development and victims' reparation have not been fully implemented. A clear case is the slow progress of land reform in rural communities. In conclusion, peace agreements are a great first step, but they only work if governments truly apply them.

07Do you think transitional justice is fairer than ordinary justice?

Model answer (B1) · Opinion + 2 Arguments + Conclusion
I think transitional and ordinary justice have different goals, so it depends on the context. Firstly, transitional justice prioritizes truth, reparation and non-repetition, which is exactly what societies after conflict really need. For example, the JEP in Colombia gives reduced sentences to those who tell the truth and repair victims. Secondly, ordinary justice would simply send everyone to prison, but that wouldn't help the country heal or move on. A clear case is South Africa, where ordinary trials would have made reconciliation impossible. In conclusion, in post-conflict contexts, transitional justice is the most appropriate model.

08How can young people contribute to building peace?

Model answer (B1) · Opinion + 2 Arguments + Conclusion
In my opinion, young people are essential for building peace because we are the future of the country. Firstly, we can contribute by educating ourselves about the conflict and learning from the past. For example, courses on Colombian history help us understand why peace is so difficult. Secondly, we can promote dialogue and tolerance in our communities through art, sport and culture. A clear case is youth groups in Medellín that organize cultural events to bring different communities together. To sum up, even small actions can help build a more peaceful society.

09What are the long-term effects of armed conflict on a country?

Model answer (B1) · Opinion + 2 Arguments + Conclusion
Armed conflict has very deep long-term effects on any country, both visible and invisible. Firstly, it destroys infrastructure, economies and entire communities, which can take decades to rebuild. For example, many Colombian rural areas still lack basic services because of the war. Secondly, it leaves invisible psychological wounds in people who lived through violence, sometimes for generations. A clear case is displaced families who still struggle with trauma and economic instability years later. In conclusion, recovering from armed conflict takes much more than just signing a peace agreement.

10Do you think the international community should intervene in armed conflicts?

Model answer (B1) · Opinion + 2 Arguments + Conclusion
Yes, I believe the international community should intervene, but mainly through peaceful means. Firstly, international support through dialogue, humanitarian aid and observers can save many lives without escalating the conflict. For example, the United Nations has supervised peace processes in many countries, including Colombia. Secondly, military intervention often causes more damage than the original conflict and creates instability for years. A clear case is some interventions in the Middle East, which generated long-term chaos. In conclusion, international support is essential, but it should always respect the sovereignty of each nation.
Part 2 · 4.5 minutes

Question & Photos

You will get an image with two photographs and a question. You have 1.5 minutes per student (4.5 minutes total) to answer the question and use the photographs to support your answer. Don't worry if the interlocutor interrupts you when time is up.

Photo comparison structure (1.5 minutes per student)

Answer the question first, then use the pictures to support what you said. Use them to defend your opinion.

1
1. Direct answer (10-15s)
Start by answering the question in ONE clear sentence. Don't begin describing the photos yet. Use 'In my opinion, ...', 'I personally believe that ...', 'Yes, I do think that ...'
2
2. Use the pictures to support your answer (60-70s)
Now use both photographs to defend your position. Compare and contrast them, but always connect what you see back to your opinion: 'Both photographs help me explain this. The first one shows ..., while the second one shows ...'
3
3. Conclusion (10-15s)
Close with a short sentence that reinforces your initial answer. Use 'To sum up, ...', 'In conclusion, ...', 'To conclude, ...'

Key phrases for Part 2

1. Answering the question (1 sentence)

  • In my opinion, ...
  • I personally believe that ...
  • From my perspective, ...
  • Yes, I do think that ...
  • No, I don't think that ...
  • My answer is that ...

2. Using the pictures to support your answer

  • While the first picture shows ..., the second one shows ...
  • As we can see in the picture on the left ...
  • Both photographs help me explain this.
  • We can clearly see this in the pictures.
  • The first picture shows ..., which supports my opinion because ...
  • The contrast between both images shows that ...
  • Both pictures together prove that ...
  • This image reminds me of ...
  • In contrast, the second photograph ...

3. Concluding

  • To sum up, ...
  • In conclusion, ...
  • To conclude, ...
  • So, I would say that ...
  • Overall, ...
OPTION 1

Globalization & Society

Is migration a human right?

Student A
Model answer
Yes, I strongly believe migration should be considered a basic human right, especially when people are escaping from war, persecution or extreme poverty. Both photographs help me explain this. The first picture shows people walking with their belongings, probably leaving their country because they have no other choice, while the second one shows a group of migrants being helped by volunteers or organizations. The first image represents the desperate decision to migrate to survive, like many Venezuelans who came to Colombia. The second image, in contrast, represents the human side of migration: solidarity, hope and a chance for a new life. The contrast between both pictures shows that migration is not a crime, but a search for safety and dignity. To sum up, migration must be respected as a human right, and the international community has the responsibility to protect those who migrate.

Is technology making the world more united or more divided?

Student B
Model answer
In my opinion, technology unites and divides us at the same time, depending on how we use it. Both photographs perfectly illustrate this idea. The first picture shows people connected through smartphones or laptops, which represents how technology brings us closer to friends and family abroad. The second one, in contrast, shows people who are physically together but each one isolated in their own screen, ignoring each other. While the first image celebrates the positive power of technology to break distances, the second one shows the dark side: emotional disconnection in real life. Both situations are very real and happen every day, even in the same family. To conclude, technology has the power to unite the world, but only if we use it consciously and not as a substitute for real human connection.

Is protecting the environment more important than economic growth?

Student C
Model answer
From my point of view, protecting the environment must come first, because without a healthy planet there can be no real economy at all. Both photographs help me explain this position. The first picture shows factories or industrial activity, which represents fast economic growth but also pollution and damage to nature. The second one, in contrast, shows a natural landscape, like a forest or a clean river, which is exactly what we should protect for future generations. The contrast between both images shows that we cannot keep choosing money over nature without serious consequences. A clear example is climate change, which already affects countries through floods, droughts and extreme weather. In conclusion, economic growth is important, but it must be sustainable to be considered real progress.
OPTION 2

Human Rights & Justice

Is it ever acceptable to break the law to fight for justice?

Student A
Model answer
In my opinion, breaking the law can sometimes be justified, but only as a last resort and when peaceful options have completely failed. Both photographs help me explain this. The first picture shows a peaceful demonstration where people protest through legal and democratic means, while the second one shows a more direct action, like blocking streets or confronting authorities. While both groups want change, their methods are very different. Personally, I prefer what the first image represents because peaceful protest builds public support; however, the second image reminds me of historical figures like Gandhi or Martin Luther King, who practiced civil disobedience to fight against deep and structural injustice. The contrast between both pictures shows that the line between legal and illegal protest depends on the context. To sum up, justice should be defended through dialogue first, and stronger actions only when nothing else works.

Can forgiveness heal a society after conflict?

Student B
Model answer
Personally, I believe forgiveness is essential to heal a society after conflict, but it must come together with truth, justice and reparation. Both photographs illustrate different moments of this process very well. The first picture shows people in pain, perhaps mourning their victims, which reminds us of the deep wounds that war leaves behind. The second one, in contrast, shows reconciliation, with people hugging or shaking hands, which represents the possibility of healing. The first image alone leaves only suffering, but the first image followed by the second shows that real change is possible after a conflict. A clear example is Colombia, where many victims have publicly forgiven former combatants in deeply moving ceremonies. To conclude, forgiveness alone is not enough, but combined with truth and reparation it can definitely heal a society.

Can a peaceful protest change a country?

Student C
Model answer
Yes, I strongly believe peaceful protest is one of the most powerful tools to transform a country. Both photographs help me support this idea. The first picture shows a large peaceful march with banners and music, which demonstrates how citizens can express themselves without violence. The second one, in contrast, shows a smaller and more emotional gathering, which reminds us that peaceful protest can also be intimate and deeply personal. While the first image represents collective strength, the second one represents individual commitment, and both are equally necessary for real change. A clear historical example is the women's rights movement, which transformed many societies without violence. In conclusion, peaceful protest can definitely change a country when citizens stay united and persistent over time.
OPTION 3

Rights & Freedoms

Is access to clean water a basic human right?

Student A
Model answer
From my perspective, access to clean water is absolutely a basic human right, because no one can live without it. Both photographs make this very clear. The first picture shows clean and abundant water, which represents a privilege that many of us take for granted in our daily lives. The second one, in contrast, shows people, often children, walking long distances or drinking dirty water just to survive. While the first photo represents normality and comfort, the second one represents a global injustice that cannot be ignored. Millions of children die every year from diseases related to dirty water, and this is completely unacceptable in the 21st century. To conclude, water is not a luxury or a privilege; it is a basic necessity for life that all governments and international organizations must guarantee.

Should governments do more to protect indigenous communities?

Student B
Model answer
Yes, I strongly believe governments must do much more to protect indigenous communities and their territories. Both photographs show contrasting realities of these communities. The first picture shows them living peacefully in their territory, in harmony with nature and keeping their traditions alive, while the second one shows the same lands being damaged by mining, deforestation or violence. While the first image represents identity and balance, the second one represents the constant threat these communities face every day. In Colombia, for example, many indigenous leaders have been killed for defending their land, which is shocking and deeply unfair. The contrast between both pictures shows what we are losing when governments do not act. To sum up, protecting indigenous communities means protecting our cultural and natural heritage as a country.

What is more important: individual freedom or public safety?

Student C
Model answer
In my opinion, individual freedom and public safety are not really opposites; they should complement each other. Both photographs help me explore this tension. The first picture shows people enjoying their freedom, like walking freely in public spaces, which represents a healthy and open society. The second one, in contrast, shows police, cameras or strict rules, which represents control and surveillance. While the first emphasizes personal liberty, the second emphasizes order. However, when governments use security as an excuse to limit basic rights, like in dictatorships, that is dangerous and unacceptable. A simple example is traffic laws: they limit our freedom a little, but make life safer for everyone. To conclude, the best society is the one that finds a healthy balance between freedom and safety.
OPTION 4

Conflict, Poverty & Equality

Can conflicts ever truly end without dialogue?

Student A
Model answer
In my opinion, conflicts cannot truly end without dialogue, because violence only creates more violence. Both photographs help me support this idea. The first picture shows people in conversation, perhaps in a peace negotiation, while the second one shows violence or military action. While the first focuses on dialogue and understanding, the second focuses only on confrontation. The first image represents the long but real path to lasting peace, while the second one represents only a temporary control of the conflict. A clear example is the Colombian peace process with the FARC, where dialogue was essential to stop a war that lasted more than 50 years. To sum up, dialogue is slow and difficult, but it is the only real way to end any conflict permanently.

How is urban poverty different from rural poverty?

Student B
Model answer
Personally, I believe urban and rural poverty are very different problems, and they need very different solutions. Both photographs show poverty, but in completely different settings. The first picture shows urban poverty, with crowded neighborhoods and informal housing in a city, while the second one shows rural poverty, with isolated houses and limited resources. While both situations are equally difficult, the challenges are not the same. In urban areas, people have access to more services but face huge inequality, competition and insecurity. In rural areas, on the other hand, people may have land and food, but very little access to education, healthcare or stable jobs. To conclude, governments must design specific policies for each context if they really want to fight poverty effectively in our country.

Is fighting for gender equality similar to fighting for racial equality?

Student C
Model answer
In my opinion, fighting for gender equality and racial equality are similar struggles because both are part of the same fight for human dignity. Both photographs show movements for equality from different angles. The first one shows women fighting for their rights, perhaps in a feminist march, while the second one shows people protesting against racial discrimination. While both movements have unique histories and experiences, they share the same essential demand: equal opportunities in jobs, education and politics. The first image speaks of the historical exclusion of women, and the second of the historical exclusion of certain ethnic groups, but in both cases the final goal is the same: justice. To sum up, they are different battles but part of the same wider struggle to build a more equal world.
OPTION 5

Global Challenges

Is pollution more visible in developed countries or in undeveloped countries?

Student A
Model answer
In my opinion, pollution is more visible in undeveloped countries, although developed countries actually pollute much more in total. Both photographs help me illustrate this paradox. The first picture shows pollution in a developed country, perhaps factories or heavy traffic, which is a real problem but somehow more 'controlled' and invisible to daily life. The second one, in contrast, shows pollution in a poor area, with trash, dirty rivers or informal waste burning right in front of people's homes. While developed countries have stricter regulations and proper waste management, in poorer regions the damage is part of the everyday landscape. A clear example is the rivers in many Latin American cities, full of plastic and chemicals. To conclude, pollution is a global problem, but its effects are deeply unequal, especially for vulnerable communities.

Is the right to privacy more important today than the right to free speech?

Student B
Model answer
From my point of view, both rights are very important, but in today's digital world, privacy is becoming more critical than ever before. Both photographs explore these two fundamental rights. The first picture shows a person being recorded or watched, perhaps by cameras or social media, which represents the constant loss of privacy in our digital era. The second one shows people expressing their opinions openly, which represents the value of free speech. While the second right is well known and defended around the world, the first one is being violated every single day, often without us even noticing. Companies and governments collect enormous amounts of data about us, including our location, messages and personal habits. In conclusion, privacy urgently needs more protection today, but free speech must also be defended at the same time.

How do peace talks and military action differ in their results?

Student C
Model answer
In my opinion, peace talks have much deeper and longer-lasting results than military action. Both photographs show different ways of dealing with conflict. The first one shows peace talks, with leaders negotiating around a table, while the second one shows military action, like soldiers or weapons. While both seek to end the conflict, the results are completely different in nature. The first image addresses the real causes of the problem and creates lasting solutions through agreement, while the second one only attacks the consequences and often produces more violence later. A clear example is the agreement between the Colombian government and the FARC, which significantly reduced violence and even brought political participation for former combatants. To sum up, talking always brings deeper and more lasting results than fighting.
Part 3: 4 minutes · 5 points

Group discussion

The evaluator assigns each student ONE option to defend. Your job is to defend your assigned position with strong arguments while engaging with what your classmates say. This part is worth 5 points: interaction and defense of your position matter more than how much you speak.

Role-based debate strategy (4 minutes)

The evaluator assigns each student ONE option to defend.

1
1. State your assigned position
Open by clearly saying which option you defend and why. Use: 'I defend option ... because ...', 'My position is that we should ...'
2
2. Give 2 strong arguments with examples
Support your position with at least two reasons and a real example. Use: 'Firstly, ... Secondly, ...', 'For example, ...'
3
3. Listen and respond to the others
Don't ignore your classmates. Acknowledge their points before you counter-argue. Use: 'I see your point, [Name], but ...', 'I respect your position, however ...'
4
4. Defend your position firmly
Don't switch sides. Show that you understood their arguments, but maintain your position with new reasons. Use: 'That's why I keep defending ...', 'My position remains the same because ...'
5
5. Close strongly
End by reinforcing why your assigned option is the best one, in 1-2 sentences.

Debate phrases

Use these phrases to defend your assigned position while engaging with your classmates' arguments. Both are essential for a high score.

Stating your position

  • My position is that we should ...
  • I strongly believe that option ... is the best.
  • From my perspective, the right choice is ...
  • I firmly believe that ..., and I support it because ...

Giving arguments

  • Firstly, ... Secondly, ...
  • The main reason is that ...
  • For example, ...
  • A clear case is ...
  • Studies/programs in ... have shown that ...

Acknowledging others' points

  • I see your point, [Name], but ...
  • I understand what you mean, however ...
  • That is a valid argument, although ...
  • I respect your position, but ...
  • You make a good point, however my position is ...

Counter-arguing politely

  • I have to disagree with that because ...
  • I'm not sure that's the best solution, because ...
  • However, my option offers ...
  • The problem with that idea is ...
  • On the contrary, my position ...

Defending your position firmly

  • That's why I'll keep defending option ...
  • My position remains the same: ...
  • I still believe my option is the strongest because ...
  • I understand, but I'll continue defending ...
  • I respect your view, but I stand by my position.

Child labor in a rural town

Option 1

In a town, many children leave school to work and support their families. Each student is assigned ONE of the following positions to defend:

1
Student A defends this
Launch community job programs offering parents stable employment to reduce the need for child labor.
2
Student B defends this
Offer financial support to families who keep their kids in school.
3
Student C defends this
Allow part-time work for children under safe conditions.
Sample debate · A defends opt 1 · B defends opt 2 · C defends opt 3
A
I strongly defend option 1: community job programs for parents. In my opinion, the real cause of child labor is that parents don't earn enough. If we give them stable jobs, families simply won't need their children to work. For example, similar programs in Brazil reduced child labor by more than 30%.
B
I see your point, A, but creating jobs for parents takes years, and meanwhile children are still leaving school. That's why I defend option 2: direct financial support to families that keep their kids in education. This solution is faster and goes straight to the source of the problem.
C
I understand both of your arguments, but I defend option 3. Sometimes families truly depend on their children's income, and banning that completely is not realistic. My option allows safe, regulated part-time work so kids can still study and contribute.
A
C, that sounds reasonable, but allowing children to work, even part-time, normalizes child labor. With my option 1, in the long term we eliminate the need for it.
B
I have to disagree with both of you. My option 2 is the only one that protects education immediately. A, your jobs take years to create; C, your part-time work still damages study time.
C
B, financial aid can create dependency. My option 3 respects the family's reality and gives children some economic independence.
A
But C, real change has to be structural. My community programs build lasting solutions, not temporary fixes.
B
A, I respect your idea, but families need help today, not in five years. That's why I'll keep defending option 2.

Rural students and access to education

Option 2

Students from rural areas have much lower access to education than urban students. Each student is assigned ONE position to defend:

1
Student A defends this
Offer scholarships for rural students to study in cities.
2
Student B defends this
Build more schools in rural areas.
3
Student C defends this
Use technology to teach students remotely.
Sample debate · A defends opt 1 · B defends opt 2 · C defends opt 3
A
I defend option 1: scholarships for rural students to study in cities. From my perspective, urban schools have better resources, more qualified teachers and stronger networks. Sending talented rural students to cities gives them real opportunities, like programs in Colombia have already shown.
B
A, I see your point, but only a few students can benefit from scholarships. I defend option 2: build more schools in rural areas. This way, ALL children, not just a small group, can access education without leaving their families and culture behind.
C
I respect both ideas, but I defend option 3. Building schools is extremely expensive and slow. With technology, we can reach thousands of rural students immediately. For example, online platforms have already transformed education in remote areas of Africa.
A
C, but rural areas often lack good internet and electricity. My scholarships at least guarantee real, in-person quality education.
B
And A, scholarships separate children from their families. My option 2 respects their identity and develops the entire community at the same time.
C
B, building schools costs millions and takes years. My option 3 is much more efficient and scalable.
A
But C, technology can never fully replace a real teacher and a real classroom.
B
Exactly, A — and that's why option 2 is the only one that gives every child a real school. I'll keep defending it.
C
I understand, but my position remains: technology is the future of inclusive education.

Floods destroying a rural region

Option 3

Frequent floods are destroying homes and crops in a rural region. Each student is assigned ONE position to defend:

1
Student A defends this
Move entire communities to safer areas.
2
Student B defends this
Invest in infrastructure like a reservoir wall and canals.
3
Student C defends this
Ban farming activities in high-risk zones.
Sample debate · A defends opt 1 · B defends opt 2 · C defends opt 3
A
I defend option 1: relocating entire communities to safer areas. People's lives must come first. Every year, families lose everything in floods. Moving them is the only way to guarantee real safety in the long term.
B
A, I see your point, but relocation destroys cultural identity and ancestral roots. I defend option 2: invest in infrastructure like reservoir walls and canals. This protects both the people and the land they have lived on for generations.
C
I respect your positions, but I defend option 3. Banning farming in high-risk zones is the most realistic solution. We cannot keep planting crops where floods constantly destroy them. It's a waste of resources.
A
C, banning farming leaves families without income. With my option 1, they get a chance to rebuild their lives in a safer place.
B
And A, your option uproots entire communities. Infrastructure is much more respectful of their history and identity. My option 2 is the most balanced.
C
B, infrastructure projects take decades and cost millions, with no guarantee they will work. My option 3 is faster and protects natural ecosystems too.
A
But C, where will those farmers go? Without my relocation plan, they have no future.
B
A, infrastructure can save the entire region without forcing anyone to leave. That's why I keep defending option 2.
C
I understand, but I'll continue defending option 3: prevention is better than reaction.

Indigenous community losing land to mining

Option 4

An indigenous group is losing its land to mining companies. Each student is assigned ONE position to defend:

1
Student A defends this
Recognize indigenous ownership legally.
2
Student B defends this
Compensate them financially but allow the mining.
3
Student C defends this
Relocate the community to a new protected area.
Sample debate · A defends opt 1 · B defends opt 2 · C defends opt 3
A
I defend option 1: full legal recognition of indigenous ownership. These communities have ancestral rights to their land. The Constitution and international treaties already protect them, so we just need to enforce these laws.
B
A, I understand your position, but mining brings important economic benefits to the country. I defend option 2: fair financial compensation while allowing the mining to continue. This balances development and respect.
C
I respect your views, but I defend option 3: relocate the community to a new protected area. Sometimes coexistence with mining is impossible. My option guarantees their safety and a healthy environment in a new location.
A
B, money cannot replace ancestral land. For indigenous communities, the territory is part of their identity and spirituality. My option 1 protects what is truly theirs.
C
Exactly, A — but staying in a polluted environment is worse. My option 3 gives them a fresh start in untouched land.
B
C, relocation is also a violation of their rights. My option 2 lets them stay AND benefit economically.
A
B, that's only true on paper. In practice, mining destroys their water, air and culture. Compensation cannot fix that.
C
I see A's point, but staying in a damaged territory is not a real solution either. Relocation can be done with consent.
A
Consent is not enough — recognition is. That's why I'll keep defending option 1.
B
And I'll keep defending option 2: a balance between development and indigenous interests.

Former guerrilla fighters returning to civilian life

Option 5

Former guerrilla fighters are trying to return to civilian life. Each student is assigned ONE position to defend:

Student A defends this
Offer them education and employment programs.
2
Student B defends this
Limit some jobs they can get.
3
Student C defends this

Sample debate · A defends opt 1 · B defends opt 2 · C defends opt 3
A
I defend option 1: full education and employment programs for ex-combatants. Reintegration only works with real opportunities. Without education and jobs, they will return to violence. Programs in Colombia have already proven this works.
B
A, I respect your position, but society also has the right to feel safe. I defend option 2: limit some sensitive jobs they can take, like in security or politics. This protects victims and builds trust slowly.
C
I understand both views, but I defend option 3: create separate communities just for ex-combatants. This avoids tensions and gives them a controlled space to rebuild their lives without conflict with civilians.

C, separating them is the same as excluding them. That's the opposite of reintegration. My option 1 makes them part of society again.

And A, total integration with no limits is risky. My option 2 is more realistic: integration with safeguards.

B, your limitations send the message that they are second-class citizens. My option 3 at least gives them dignity in their own community.
A
C, isolation has never produced peace. Real reconciliation needs ex-combatants AND victims to share spaces.
B
A, sharing all spaces is too fast. We need time and clear boundaries, like my option 2 proposes.
C
I understand, but I keep defending option 3: a transition space before full reintegration.
A
And I'll keep defending option 1: real reintegration starts with full opportunities and trust.
